title: Modelling Drainage‐Induced Transitions in Irish Peatlands: A Process‐Based Approach to Ecosystem Stability
content:
ABSTRACT

Peatlands are globally significant ecosystems, valued for their role in carbon sequestration, water regulation and biodiversity support. However, historical drainage and emerging climate pressures are threatening their long-term resilience. Resilience here refers to the ability to retain a saturated, peat-forming state. Drainage can push peatlands beyond tipping points into alternative stable states, such as forest. These thresholds vary by peatland type and climatic region. In this study, we apply an enhanced version of the PeatScapes numerical model to evaluate how artificial drainage affects the hydrological stability of Ireland's two dominant peatland types: raised bogs and blanket bogs. Raised bogs showed greater sensitivity to active ditch drainage than blanket bogs, with drainage effects weakening as distance increased. Following drainage removal, raised-bog biomass remained above the undrained control after 500 years, whereas blanket-bog biomass approached it. These contrasting responses underscore the need for peatland-type-specific restoration strategies. By identifying modelled hydrological and spatial thresholds, the study provides a framework for assessing drainage-induced degradation and informing peatland conservation and restoration. The findings support policy and land management efforts to mitigate peatland degradation and reinforce their climate-buffering capacity.
